Lunar Landing Site Navigator
NASA Space Apps Challenge

Team: Yassen Ahmed, Omar Ahmed, Hazem Adel, Abdrhman Mohmed, Marwan Ali, and Ayten Saad.

We developed the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a simulation-based tool that helps mission planners evaluate Moon landing sites before sending a spacecraft. It addresses three major risks: dangerous terrain, communication loss when Earth is out of sight, and power failure caused by extreme temperatures and limited sunlight.

The platform features an interactive 3D Moon powered by NASA data. It calculates solar and Earth angles, solar power availability, and surface temperature in real time. Users can explore lunar terrain, adjust the simulation speed up to 86,400×, and analyze conditions through live telemetry, charts, and a 30-day sunlight map.

An AI-powered feasibility score evaluates five factors: slope, lighting, power, communication, and thermal conditions. It produces a score from 0 to 100, classifying sites as Safe, Caution, or High Risk.

During testing at Shackleton Crater’s rim, the system achieved 75%, revealing a critical communication risk despite favorable lighting, power, and thermal conditions.

Our mission is to reduce landing failures, communication loss, and power shortages by turning complex lunar data into clear decisions within seconds.

Know the risk before you land.
details:
# Lunar Landing Site Navigator: Testing the Landing on the Screen, Not on the Moon

NASA Space Apps Challenge — Team: Yassen Ahmed, Omar Ahmed, Hazem Adel, Abdrhman Mohmed, Marwan Ali, Ayten Saad

Landing on the Moon is a gamble without data. A bad slope or a rock field can destroy a lander at touchdown. Earth can slip out of view for more than two weeks, cutting off all contact. And the wrong sunlight timing combined with −173 °C lunar nights can drain a battery before the mission ever gets going. Too often, teams only discover how risky a site is after the fact — when it is already too late.

That is the gap the Lunar Landing Site Navigator was built to close. The tool simulates a landing before the rocket flies, combining real NASA data on the Moon, Sun, and Earth with a live 3D environment and an AI feasibility score.

At its core is a real-time 3D Moon that calculates Sun and Earth angles, available solar power, and surface temperature for any candidate site. Users can rotate the model, face the Sun or Earth, and speed up the simulation clock to 86,400× to compress an entire lunar day into seconds. Live telemetry reports Sun and Earth angles, power, and temperature as they change, while charts and a sunlight map project solar power across a 30-day window.

Those inputs feed a five-part feasibility check — slope, lighting, power, communications, and thermal — which produces a single score from 0 to 100. A score of 70 or above reads Safe; 40 to 69 means Caution, landing is possible but risks remain; anything under 40 is High risk. A test run at the Shackleton crater rim, for example, returned a 75% score with full marks for lighting, power, and thermal — yet zero for Earth line-of-sight, with Earthrise still two and a half days away. That is precisely the kind of hidden trade-off the tool is designed to expose.

The payoff is practical: risky slopes and hazards get flagged before launch, Earth visibility windows become visible in advance so communications can be planned, and landing times can be chosen with enough sunlight and safe temperatures. Fewer crashes, less signal loss, less power failure — all decided on the screen rather than on the lunar surface.

The project runs a full site assessment in seconds across arbitrary coordinates and dates, replacing what would otherwise be hours of manual cross-referencing. Looking ahead, the team plans to add automated hazard classification from higher-resolution imagery, multi-site comparison ranking, and real relay satellite ephemerides for more accurate communication windows.

The message is simple: know the risk before you land.

---

Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
